text: Hi, Maya, how has the past week been since we last met? Honestly, a little uneven. I felt organized at the beginning of the week, then work became busy and I started feeling behind. When did you first notice that shift Tuesday afternoon. My manager asked for an update in a meeting, and I had not finished the draft I wanted to show. What went through your mind in that moment, I thought. Everyone can tell I'm not keeping up. I felt my face get hot and I could not focus on the rest of the meeting. That sounds uncomfortable. What did you do after the meeting ended? I went back to my desk and tried to work faster, but I kept rereading the same email. Later I skipped my walk and worked through dinner. Did working longer make you feel more caught up? Not really. I finished a few small things, but then I was tired and more critical of myself. You are noticing that the pressure to catch up can sometimes make it harder to concentrate. Yes, it turns into this loop where I am anxious because I have work to do, and then I am slower because I am anxious. Let us slow down that moment in the meeting. What evidence did you have that people thought you were not keeping up? I did not have much evidence. My manager just asked a normal question. One co-worker even said the timeline looked reasonable. And what evidence pointed in a different direction? I had completed most of the research and I had already told my manager that the draft would be ready Wednesday. I guess I treated one question like proof that I was failing. That is a useful distinction. How did you respond to yourself later that evening? I was pretty harsh. I said I was lazy even though I had been working all day. If a friend described the same situation, what might you say to them? I would probably say that one delayed draft does not erase all the work they have done and that taking a break might help them finish it. How does it feel to apply that same response to yourself, a little strange but calmer. I do not fully believe it yet, but I can see it is more fair. That is enough for now. We are practicing a more balanced response, not forcing yourself to feel perfectly confident. Did you have any moments this week that felt restorative? On Saturday morning, I made coffee and sat outside before looking at my phone. It was only about 20 minutes, but I felt like myself again. What made that time different? There was no goal attached to it. I was not trying to improve anything or catch up. I was just paying attention to the weather and my dog running around. That sounds like a good example of intentional rest. Would it be realistic to build in another small window like that this week? Maybe. I could take 10 minutes outside after lunch on Tuesday and Thursday. I usually scrolled at my desk instead. What could make that plan easier to follow? I can put a reminder on my calendar and leave my headphones at my desk, so I do not turn the walk into another task. Good Earlier you mentioned skipping dinner. How has eating and sleep been this week? Sleep was OK most nights, around 7 hours. I ate regularly except Tuesday when I was too wound up to notice I was hungry. Were there any warning signs before you reached that point? My shoulders were tight. I was holding my breath, and I kept telling myself I could not stop until the draft was done. Could those be cues to pause for two minutes, drink water, or check whether you need food? Yes, I think that would help. It sounds simple, but I usually wait until I feel terrible. Many people do. The goal is to notice the earlier signals, not to respond perfectly every time. I like that. It feels less like another rule I can fail. Before we finish, let us summarize your plan for the week. When you notice the thought, Everyone can tell I am not keeping up, what will you try? I will ask what evidence I actually have and remind myself that a question is not proof that I am failing. And for rest, I will take a 10 minute walk after lunch Tuesday and Thursday without my phone. What is one small way to support yourself if work gets intense again? I will pause before working through dinner, check in with my body, and send a realistic update instead of silently panicking. That is a thoughtful plan. How are you feeling as we end today? More steady. I still expect work to be busy, but I have a few things to try instead of just pushing harder. I am glad we can review what you noticed next time and adjust the plan together.

clinical_note.name: Chief Complaint
items: Anxiety and work-related stress

clinical_note.name: History Of Present Illness
items: The patient presents for follow-up regarding anxiety and work-related stress.
They report an uneven week, initially feeling organized but becoming overwhelmed when work became busy.
The patient describes a specific incident on Tuesday afternoon during a meeting when their manager asked for an update on a draft that was not yet finished.
This triggered feelings of inadequacy, with the patient thinking "everyone can tell I'm not keeping up."
They experienced facial flushing and difficulty focusing during the meeting.
Afterward, the patient attempted to work faster but found themselves rereading the same email repeatedly.
They skipped their usual walk and worked through dinner, which did not make them feel more caught up and instead left them tired and more critical of themselves.
The patient describes a pattern where anxiety about work leads to decreased productivity, which in turn increases anxiety.
They acknowledge that the pressure to catch up makes it harder to concentrate.

When asked to examine the evidence for their belief that others noticed they were not keeping up, the patient realized they had little evidence — their manager had asked a normal question and a coworker had commented that the timeline looked reasonable.
They had completed most of the research and had already informed their manager the draft would be ready Wednesday.
The patient recognized they had treated one question as proof of failure.
Later that evening, the patient was self-critical, calling themselves "lazy" despite having worked all day.
When asked to apply the same compassion they would show a friend, the patient acknowledged this approach felt "a little strange but calmer" and more fair.
The patient reports a restorative experience on Saturday morning, spending 20 minutes outside with coffee and their dog without a goal or phone.
They felt "like myself again" during this time.
Regarding sleep, the patient reports it was "ok most nights" with approximately 7 hours of sleep.
They ate regularly except on Tuesday, when they were too wound up to notice hunger.
The patient identified early warning signs of stress including tight shoulders and holding their breath.

clinical_note.name: Review Of Systems
items: Constitutional: Reports normal sleep (approximately 7 hours most nights)
Psychiatric: Reports anxiety, reports difficulty concentrating, reports self-critical thoughts

clinical_note.name: Past Social History
items: Employed in a professional role with a manager and coworkers
Has a dog

clinical_note.name: Assessment
items: 1. Anxiety

clinical_note.name: Plan
items:
Anxiety:
- Cognitive reframing: when experiencing the thought "everyone can tell I'm not keeping up," patient will ask what evidence they actually have and remind themselves that a question is not proof of failure
- Self-compassion practice: applying the same understanding to self as would to a friend (e.g., recognizing that one delayed draft does not erase all work done)
- Intentional rest: scheduled 10-minute walks after lunch on Tuesdays and Thursdays without phone or headphones
- Early warning sign recognition: when noticing shoulder tension or holding breath, patient will pause for two minutes, drink water, and check in with body needs (hunger, hydration)
- Communication strategy: when work becomes intense, patient will pause before working through dinner, check in with body, and send a realistic update instead of silently panicking
- Discussed the concept of intentional rest and its benefits
- Explored the difference between productive work and counterproductive "pushing harder" when anxious
- Encouraged patient to notice early physical warning signs of stress rather than waiting until feeling "terrible"
- Reinforced that the goal is to notice signals and practice a more balanced response, not to respond perfectly every time
- Review patient's progress with new strategies at next session and adjust plan as needed
